item.title: Asymmetry between the major parties fries the circuits of the mainstream press - PressThink
item.description: Rosen analyzes the challenges faced by mainstream political journalism during the 2016 US presidential election campaign, particularly in covering Donald Trump. Rosen argues that the traditional journalistic framework, based on the assumption of symmetry between the two major parties, is inadequate for understanding Trump's unconventional candidacy and the resulting asymmetric polarization. He proposes three key propositions: 1) Political journalism relies on a shared mental picture of politics that assumes similar actors with 'warring philosophies'; 2) This symmetry is disrupted by the Republican Party's extreme stance and Trump's disregard for facts and norms; and 3) The media's failure to adapt to this asymmetry resembles 'technical debt', leading to a distorted representation of reality.

item.title: So I will try to explain why the Trump candidacy has been so confounding to our political press. - PressThink
item.description: Rosen analyzes the changing dynamics of political journalism in the context of the 2016 US presidential election, particularly the impact of Donald Trump's campaign. Rosen argues that the traditional 'laws of political gravity' governing campaign coverage, based on shared assumptions within the political class and media, have broken down. This breakdown is attributed to Trump's disregard for established norms and the media's struggle to adapt, leading to homogeneity in coverage and a lack of clear purpose. Rosen contrasts this with the approach of Jorge Ramos, who demonstrates a clear sense of purpose and audience representation, illustrating an alternative model for political journalism.

item.title: The Pub #43: Why public media are sponsoring polls, and how a CBC video went viral
item.description: The Pub podcast episode opens with Rosen's Twitter critique of WBUR for sponsoring horse-race polls and asks how polling fits with public media's mission. WBUR's Sam Fleming responds to Rosen's argument; the episode also features Marketplace host Kai Ryssdal.

item.title: Adapting Journalism to the Digital Space
item.description: NYU's Studio 20: Digital First program prepares the next generation of journalists for the digital age by focusing on practical, project-based learning in collaboration with established media companies and digital startups. The program aims to equip students with skills to innovate in digital newsrooms, bridge business, editorial, tech, and audience challenges, and regain public trust.

item.title: Verstehen, was den Journalismus derzeit verändert
item.description: Journalism is undergoing significant changes, and many struggle to understand them, often getting caught between condemning the new digital landscape or clinging to the old ways. The core issue lies in the fact that journalists are products of the changing society they are trying to understand, making it hard for them to objectively assess their own role. To better comprehend these shifts, media houses and journalists must observe society, technology, science, economics, and politics, recognizing patterns and connections rather than judging individual phenomena. Breaking down silos and fostering collaboration among various professionals is crucial to understanding and shaping the future of journalism and remaining relevant in a constantly evolving world.

item.title: Comment être au courant de ce qui change le journalisme ?
item.description: To stay informed about the evolving landscape of journalism, one should utilize various resources. Newsletters like La Matinale du Monde and Le 5 à 7 de l’AFP provide key information. Specialized websites such as Journalisme.com and Arrêt sur images offer in-depth analysis. Books like “Le Journalisme sans journalistes” and “La Fabrication de l’information” offer deeper insights. Blogs and Twitter accounts, including those of Daniel Schneidermann and Slate.fr, provide real-time updates and commentary.

item.title: The Studio 2.0 Program at NYU (directed by Jay Rosen and Clay Shirky) once again presents Open Studio Night!
item.description: Studio 2.0 at NYU, co-directed by Jay Rosen and Clay Shirky, is hosting its second Open Studio Night. The event allows the program's twelve students to showcase their projects focused on the future of news, providing opportunities for interaction, feedback, and discussion. Attendees can learn about emerging trends in journalism. The event will be held on Wednesday, November 19, 2014, at the Studio 2.0 Room in New York, NY, and requires an RSVP. Studio 2.0 emphasizes experimentation and creation, encouraging students to build prototypes and design new services in response to changes in journalism. The program prioritizes invention and creation alongside critical thinking, with a focus on practical application.

item.title: Rosen's Trust Puzzler: What Explains Falling Confidence in the Press? - PressThink
item.description: Rosen explores the declining public trust in news media despite improvements in journalistic professionalism. Rosen presents several competing explanations, including the general decline in trust across institutions, the negative influence of bad actors in media, accusations of liberal bias, strategic manipulation of journalists ('working the refs'), and a potential misalignment between journalistic professionalization and public needs. Rosen concludes that none of these explanations fully capture the complexity of the issue and invites further discussion.

item.title: Open Studio Night, 2013: where our students present their final projects
item.description: These twelve presented their final projects in front of an East Village crowd with friends, family and digital journalism people from the New York media world. Boryana created an engagement strategy for Narratively’s core readership, which could expand their content outside the New York City area. Danielle Powell / Al Jazeera America : The problem: Repurposing TV documentary by putting it online is lame: there has to be a better way!

item.title: When quoting both sides and leaving it there is the riskier call
item.description: Rosen critiques the 'he said, she said' approach in journalism, arguing that in situations where facts are verifiable, presenting both sides equally can be reckless and even misleading. Rosen uses examples from the New York Times' coverage of plagiarism accusations against a book and the BBC's handling of climate change reporting to illustrate how clinging to false equivalence can confer legitimacy on false claims and distort the truth. Rosen contends that the old standard of 'no position' is increasingly risky and that newsrooms need to evolve beyond this approach.

item.title: This is just a stub for a PressThink post
item.description: Jay Rosen plans to expand a post regarding The New York Times' need to explain why it published a front-page story about Russian officials releasing photos of soldiers in Ukraine that later proved false. Rosen's post initially appeared on Facebook and criticizes the newspaper's inadequate correction, specifically pointing out the lack of explanation for the new evidence and the Times' downplaying of its original assertion that Russia released the photos. Rosen contends that this failure hinders readers' ability to assess the images' credibility and suggests the State Department's reliance on the Times compromises the paper's value.

item.title: Pierre Omidyar plunges first $50m into media venture with Glenn Greenwald
item.description: Pierre Omidyar, founder of eBay, is investing $50 million (the first tranche of a $250 million commitment) in a new journalism venture, First Look Media, with Glenn Greenwald. This venture will consist of both a non-profit (501(c)(3)) news organization and a for-profit media technology company. The for-profit entity will support the non-profit's independent journalism. The venture's structure is compared to that of the Guardian Media Group and Bloomberg News, with Jay Rosen, a NYU professor advising the venture, highlighting its innovative funding model.

item.title: A First Look at NewCo's structure - PressThink
item.description: Pierre Omidyar's $50 million investment establishes First Look Media, a new media organization comprised of both for-profit and non-profit entities. The non-profit arm will focus on independent, public-interest journalism, while the for-profit arm will develop new media technologies. Profits from the for-profit entity will support the non-profit's journalistic mission, offering a new model for sustainable, independent journalism.

item.title: A News Organization That Rejects the View From Nowhere
item.description: Rosen discusses a new $250 million news organization founded by Pierre Omidyar that will not adhere to traditional journalistic objectivity. The article features an interview with Jay Rosen, a media theorist and critic of the 'View From Nowhere,' who is joining the organization as an advisor. Rosen discusses the challenges and implications of implementing his 'View From Somewhere' theory, which emphasizes transparency about journalists' perspectives and priors, while maintaining high verification standards. The interview explores the tension between individual journalist perspectives, organizational viewpoints, and the need for editorial oversight, touching upon issues of ideological diversity, accountability, and the role of readers.

item.title: Studio 20
item.description: ¶ ● (L-R) Students Nuha Abujaber, Jesse Kipp, and Simran Khosla From Amy Webb, Head of Webbmedia Group This past spring, Studio 20 students in their second term partnered with a diverse group of companies for a project focusing on networked reporting. I think it shows the interconnectedness between a lot of companies and makes you realize it’s not just a series of start-ups going through similar cycles; there’s actually many key players and investors who really shape the ecosystem. note: NYU instructor Jonathan Soma will be featured in an upcoming Q&A on this blog soon - stay tuned.)

item.title: Open Studio night: Dec. 12, 6 to 8 pm at NYU. Would you like to come?
item.description: And… Josh Benton, director of Harvard’s Nieman Lab, will present his slide show: “The Year in Innovation." Our graduating students present their final projects in innovation, which they have spent six months working on. So please make plans to be there: Thursday, December 12 at NYU Journalism, 20 Cooper Square, New York, NY, 7th floor.

item.title: Old testament and new testament journalism - PressThink
item.description: The article contrasts two forms of journalism, "old testament" and "new testament," characterized by political argument intertwined with information and the separation of facts and values, respectively. It argues that both forms are necessary and that the rise of the internet has allowed the old testament form to gain new life, while weaknesses in new testament traditions have been exposed. Rosen sees a potential reconciliation and détente between the two, acknowledging the virtues and vices of each.

item.title: Studio 20
item.description: Some quotes from the conversation: “I have a habit of creating jobs for myself.” “The best journalists are marketers.” “I get so many ideas on things from Twitter.” “Suggest an alternative and how you’re two steps ahead - that’s golden.” Professor Jay Rosen was interviewed by Callie in 2010. Last night, the tables were turned as Rosen discussed ideas around innovation (and a bit of politics too), with the final takeaway being: Figure out what needs to be done and do it, regardless of whether it fits with the “image” you have of yourself and your position. That, right there, is the encapsulation of what we do at Studio 20.

item.title: The NSA's next move: silencing university professors?
item.description: A Johns Hopkins professor's blog post criticizing the NSA was requested to be taken down by the university's dean, raising concerns about academic freedom. The request, seemingly originating from the university's Applied Physics Laboratory with ties to the NSA, was later retracted after media attention, highlighting the vulnerability of academic freedom to government pressure and the university's initial failure to uphold its principles.

item.title: The awayness problem
item.description: An analysis of what Rosen calls "the awayness problem" in journalism — how the press can be physically present yet intellectually absent from the stories it covers. Published in Columbia Journalism Review.

item.title: Studio 20 gets an assignment from Quartz News
item.description: ¶ ● Studio 20 gets an assignment from Quartz News These specs were sent by the editors of Quartz to Professor Jay Rosen as part of Studio 20’s networked reporting project in spring 2013. Jay Rosen responded with his presentation, Designs for a Networked Beat , May 13, 2013. The problem: As well as Quartz’s longer-term obsessions, we often obsess on shorter-term stories that turn into big news for a few days or weeks, but that we don’t know in advance are going to become big.

item.title: Studio 20's Networked Reporting Project
item.description: We had six partners: ProPublica, The Wall Street Journal Social Media Desk, Mashable.com’s gaming beat, PandoDaily.com, Fast Company and Quartz News (qz.com). Each came to class and explained the problems they have making more productive use of a networked approach. The Wall Street Journal Social Media desk A tool for locating likely sources within an established Twitter network.

item.title: Open Studio Night: An Invitation.
item.description: PUSH worked with Ebony.com as a test client to develop an original man-on-the-street video series, among other creative multimedia projects. The new template will encourage contributors to package existing content (text and images) into video news clips. She has been working on funding, design and community outreach, including advisory sessions with Homicide Watch.

item.title: Lewis Dvorkin fields some good questions from Studio 20
item.description: ¶ ● Lewis Dvorkin fields some good questions from Studio 20 Lewis Dvorkin recently stopped in Studio 20 to talk with first year masters students about innovation in the digital age. “We felt like equals, which is really cool when you’re talking to the head honcho of online media at Forbes,” notes Studio-20er Simran Khosla . Well, it’s far more than making phone calls, writing a story and going home.

item.title: Ungovernable reality, not Candy Crowley, threatens Obama and Romney
item.description: Rosen analyzes the dynamics between presidential campaigns, the Commission on Presidential Debates, and journalists moderating debates. It highlights the tension between the desire of campaigns to control the debate format and the journalist's role in pressing for answers and holding candidates accountable. Rosen explores different moderator styles, from the 'Vanishing Moderator' to a more active interlocutor, and argues that the lack of consensus on the ideal approach reflects a deeper question about whether presidential power needs an independent check.

item.title: Final projects for Studio 20 students: they're all about incremental innovation. All have media partners.
item.description: Working with a media partner, they each have to design and execute their own project in innovation. Laura Edwins is partnering with The Christian Science Monitor in Boston to build a user engagement strategy for their politics blog, DC Decoder . The new template will encourage contributors to package existing contents (text and image) into video news clips.

item.title: Studio 20
item.description: ¶ ● The skills Studio 20 students have and want to gain Jay Rosen asked the incoming class of Studio 20 students to participate in an inventory: the skills they came in with and the skills they most wanted to acquire during their 16-month graduate program. Then they had to come up with a way of representing it that tapped into some of those skills, plus they had to introduce themselves and their backgrounds. (Asked what the takeaway was, the students said: next time, don’t build it in flash!)

item.title: Kevin Convey brings innovation from the newsroom to the classroom
item.description: That’s when I got a job as Editor in Chief of The New York Daily News . What I’m doing is talking to them about innovation and disruption in the news industry. I think that everything is going well, but my students will ultimately be the ones to judge me.

item.title: Studio 20 prof brings us 'Obama Revealed'
item.description: ¶ ● Studio 20 prof brings us 'Obama Revealed' A quick programming note… Professor Jason Samuels’ latest documentary project is scheduled to air on CNN tonight at 8:00 p.m. EST. The program includes original sit-down interviews with President Obama, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Former White House Chief of Staff Rahm Emanuel, Former Director of White House Economic Council Larry Summers, the former Chairs of the President’s Council of Economic Advisers Austan Goolsbee and Christina Romer, Senior Campaign Strategist David Axelrod, Senior Adviser Valerie Jarrett, House Speaker John Boehner, Senator Olympia Snowe, Obama biographer and Washington Post associate editor David Maraniss, Rice University Professor and Historian Douglas Brinkley, New York Times Chief Washington Correspondent David Sanger, former personal aide Reggie Love and Obama supporter Velma Hart. Watch, Tweet, and let us know what you think: @profsamuels_nyu @studio20NYU 0 notes

item.title: This Year's Studio 20 Summer Gigs
item.description: = Silva Shih has spent her summer working with NYU Stern’s economics professor David Backus on a video project, while also reporting for Taiwanese media. = This summer, Tando Ntunja is interning at Global Grind , a Russell Simmons-owned online entertainment journalism site that focuses on the confluence between hip-hop and pop culture. She has focused on creating compelling health coverage and promoting news content using the right social media tools.

item.title: David Holmes explains it all -- in song
item.description: “I mean charting your own path, with or without the help of an established journalistic institution, and, most importantly, not waiting for someone else’s permission to do something innovative.” And while Holmes has found success with some big-name media outlets, that may not be the only way to get your ideas out there. Any schlub like me can create a YouTube account and spit out content I think might be beneficial to viewers. While the success of our videos has largely been driven through more institutional channels, guys like Kevin T. Porter who created the Sorkinisms supercut will tell you that if a video is well-timed and entertaining (and in our case, we’ll add “informative” to the list), all it takes is a community on Twitter or Reddit to discover it in order to attract a huge audience.

item.title: Covering Wicked Problems - PressThink
item.description: Rosen introduces the distinction between "tame" and "wicked" problems, arguing that many issues facing society, such as climate change and failing public schools, are wicked problems—complex, ill-defined, and resistant to traditional solutions. The article proposes a new journalistic beat focused on wicked problems, suggesting that it should be a network, pattern-based, global, and reliant on diverse perspectives rather than solely on expert opinions. This beat would highlight the process of grappling with these problems, focusing on narratives of getting stuck and getting unstuck, and acknowledging the role of denial in hindering progress.

item.title: Four Types of Scoops
item.description: Jonathan Stray identifies four ways journalists beat the competition: exclusive leaks from confidential sources, enterprise reporting through public records and legwork, expert interviews, and original analysis. He argues that enterprise reporting — digging through obscure records and finding on-the-record sources — is the most valuable form, yet also the most threatened by the economics of modern journalism.

item.title: Verification in reverse': A chat with Jay Rosen
item.description: This article presents a conversation between Scott Rosenberg and Jay Rosen about "verification in reverse," a process where previously established truths are challenged. The discussion centers on a Huffington Post article concerning a letter from NASA retirees criticizing the agency's climate research. Rosen defines verification in reverse and explains how it poses a significant problem for journalists who must balance reporting controversies with upholding factual accuracy. He highlights the conflict between science journalists who consider climate change a settled issue and political journalists who focus on partisan debates, emphasizing the reluctance of many political journalists to confront climate change denialism. Rosen suggests that journalists should not only investigate what happened but also determine whether denialism is involved and treat this as news itself.

item.title: Maybe your site should be home to a Studio 20 project
item.description: We dispense with cliches like “Why didn’t the news industry invent Facebook?” and plunge our diversely-talented students into real world projects where they can test their ideas against all the practical constraints that make it hard to do new things in journalism. Studio 20 graduate students are trained to understand the partner’s editorial strategy and business model first. However, we do respect your time and when there is a meeting our people are hyper-prepared.

item.title: Anatomy of a Facebook Fail (mine)
item.description: Rosen recounts a Facebook mishap involving an event invitation. Intending to invite spouses of friends using the "suggest invitees" feature, they accidentally invited thousands of people, including all their friends and their spouses' friends. This resulted in a flood of notifications and inquiries. Due to the event's public setting, Rosen couldn't uninvite everyone or delete the event initially. With a friend's help, they changed the privacy settings and deleted the event. Rosen shares lessons learned, including the importance of caution with the "select all" feature, carefully checking privacy settings, acting quickly to address problems, seeking help when needed, and following up with those legitimately invited. Rosen encourages others to share their social media failures.

item.title: First Year Studio 20-er Anjali Mullany Makes Moves
item.description: I’ve been responsible for real-time reporting, engagement, and crowdsourcing efforts at the Daily News since late 2009, though as time went on it became a newsroom-wide effort. I start my new job as social media editor at Fast Company the end of April. Fast Company is a great environment for someone who wants room to experiment and expand their repertoire—a very cool place.

item.title: Adapting Journalism to the Web
item.description: Jay Rosen and Ethan Zuckerman discuss the transformation of journalism in the digital age. Rosen argues that the internet has democratized the freedom of the press, but also fragmented the mass audience. Zuckerman raises concerns about citizen journalism and the potential for misinformation, citing the Mike Daisey scandal. They explore the evolving roles of journalists, the importance of transparency, and the challenges of echo chambers. Rosen emphasizes that journalism is about relaying facts, distinguishing it from political rhetoric. Both discuss the need to support journalists in a changing media landscape and encourage greater public participation and civic dialogue.

item.title: The Man Behind the News Songs
item.description: Watch below: We interviewed Holmes about his newfound success and what it feels like to be working in a relatively new news genre. When the “ Building a Better Explainer ” project came along with ProPublica, I figured, “well people really like the bed bugs song, so I’ll make a song about fracking and see what happens.” We found some great animators, and everything that could go right did. For this last video, Krishanan Vasudevan, and Sharon Shattuck, both graduates of NYU’s News & Doc program, did the animation.

item.title: Professor Samuels at SXSW: Black in America/Silicon Valley, the Aftermath
item.description: The conversation it sparked over diversity—or lack thereof—in Silicon is still being hashed out. “To my surprise our Black In America documentary panel was standing room only. The documentary continues to resonate far beyond my expectations in terms of impact and awareness.

item.title: NPR Tackles 'False Equivalence'
item.description: The article discusses NPR's new guidelines aimed at addressing "false equivalence" in journalism, where equal weight is given to opposing sides of a story, even if one side is factually inaccurate. The author praises NPR's commitment to prioritizing truth and fairness to the truth over the appearance of balance, but also includes a reader's example illustrating the ongoing challenges of avoiding false equivalence, particularly in contentious issues.

item.title: Did the Citizens Agenda influence the GOP debate in Arizona?
item.description: Rosen discusses the Citizens Agenda project undertaken by The Guardian and NYU's Studio 20 program to analyze the questions asked at the Republican presidential debates. The study found that the debates focused heavily on certain topics while neglecting others, highlighting a divergence between the press agenda and the concerns of citizens. Rosen advocates for a greater focus on issues like healthcare, Super PACs, and science and technology in future debates.

item.title: The Citizens’ Agenda Round 1: #unasked Questions in GOP Debates
item.description: We also found only two questions about climate change, four mentioning the Arab Spring, and one on women’s rights beyond abortion. And we wondered: were people eager to hear more about these scantly covered issues? What is your opinion on food labeling?” — Sewassbe, via comments Thanks to a stellar interactive feature from the Guardian team, readers could also vote up what topics they wanted to hear more about on site.

item.title: NPR Tries to Get its Pressthink Right
item.description: This article analyzes NPR's revised ethics handbook, highlighting its shift from a credibility-focused, defensive approach to a more affirmative focus on producing trust and prioritizing the audience. The key change involves a rejection of 'he said, she said' journalism in favor of prioritizing fairness to the truth, even if it means acknowledging imbalances in evidence. The author praises this evolution, arguing that it empowers those within NPR who strive for improved journalistic practices.

item.title: (More) Studio 20 Grads Settle into their New Jobs!
item.description: I think that Studio 20 teaches you how to be independent and quick on your feet. Lately we’ve been working on personal branding training for our reporters and editors, where we really get to inform them and help them understand how to optimize the ways that different networks are used. I regularly help brainstorm ideas with Anjali about how we can better engage and inform the Daily News community as a whole.

item.title: Have the 839 GOP debate questions reflected the 'citizens agenda'?
item.description: The article critiques the Republican primary debates of 2012, highlighting the disparity between the questions asked by journalists and the issues that voters are actually concerned about. It discusses a study by NYU's Studio 20 analyzing the topics covered in the debates and contrasts them with a "citizens agenda" approach, which prioritizes the concerns of the electorate. Rosen proposes shifting campaign coverage to better reflect the priorities of the public and encourages readers to suggest topics they want the candidates to discuss.

item.title: Studio 20 Grads Settle into their New Jobs!
item.description: I lead a team of editors to write, edit, blog, publish, and curate news that interest our audience, Arabic language speakers all over the world. A big part of it is keeping an eye on the website’s numbers—the page views, unique visitors, top stories, etc.—and then seeing how we can use that data to create better, more engaging content. I work on a small team that conducts something called “user research” in order to help make our digital product offerings better.

item.title: A Brief Theory of the Republican Party (2012)
item.description: Before the 1980s, the Republican Party was similar to the Democratic Party. The Great Realignment saw Ronald Reagan build a new coalition consisting of socially conservative Christians, the wealthy, and the Southern working class, united by exploiting social tensions. The Republican Party then shifted its focus from economic to social issues, fostering resentment towards groups considered the "liberal elite." After Reagan, the party found a new unifying force in attacking the government, though this created internal tension regarding popular programs. The Republican Party is now in crisis, divided by its inability to shrink the government while still protecting popular programs. The party's future is uncertain, possibly fracturing or fading away without a new way to unite its factions.

item.title: Studio 20
item.description: ¶ ● A student reflects on her time at Studio 20. Shortly after, she wrote this post: My Time in Studio 20. “With newly established programs, you can either come out of it with a type of education no one has had before, or you can have an awful experience of a program that’s not well thought out.” Read the rest .
